title: Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy
competency: Describe kinetic energy as the movement of objects or particles, and potential energy as energy stored due to the position of objects or particles; and identify examples of everyday situations that demonstrate kinetic energy being transformed to potential energy and potential energy being transformed to kinetic energy.
objectives: Define kinetic energy and potential energy.
Explain the factors that affect the amount of kinetic and potential energy.
Describe the transformation between kinetic and potential energy in a system.
Relate the Law of Conservation of Energy to everyday examples.
introduction: Energy is the capacity to do work. In mechanical systems, energy exists in two primary forms: Kinetic Energy (energy in motion) and Potential Energy (stored energy). These two forms are constantly shifting back and forth as objects change their speed or their height above the ground.
content:
1. Potential Energy (PE)

Potential Energy is energy that is stored in an object due to its position or state. The most common form in this level is Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE).

  • Factors: GPE depends on the object's mass (m), the acceleration due to gravity (g), and its height (h) relative to a reference point.
  • Formula: PE = mgh
  • An object held higher from the ground has more potential energy than an object held lower.

2. Kinetic Energy (KE)

Kinetic Energy is the energy possessed by an object in motion. Every moving object, from a planet to a subatomic particle, has kinetic energy.

  • Factors: KE depends on the object's mass (m) and its velocity (v).
  • Formula: KE = ½mv²
  • Because velocity is squared in the formula, doubling the speed of an object quadruples its kinetic energy.

3. Energy Transformation

Energy is never created nor destroyed; it only changes form. This is the Law of Conservation of Energy.

  • PE to KE: When an object falls, its height decreases (losing PE) while its speed increases (gaining KE).
  • KE to PE: When an object is thrown upward, its speed decreases (losing KE) while its height increases (gaining PE).

examples.title: The Roller Coaster
examples.description: As the car is pulled to the top of the first hill, it gains maximum Potential Energy. As it drops, that PE is transformed into Kinetic Energy, reaching maximum speed at the bottom.

examples.title: A Pendulum
examples.description: At the highest point of its swing, the pendulum has maximum PE and zero KE. At the lowest point (middle), it has maximum KE and minimum PE.

keyTerms.definition: The standard unit of energy in the International System of Units.
Energy stored in an object due to its vertical position or height.
The sum of potential energy and kinetic energy in a system.

keyConcepts: Potential energy is 'hidden' energy; kinetic energy is 'active' energy.
Energy transformation occurs continuously in moving systems.
The total mechanical energy remains constant in a frictionless system.
summary: Potential energy is stored based on an object's position, while kinetic energy is the energy of motion. In any moving system, energy transitions between these two forms. The total amount of energy remains the same, illustrating the Law of Conservation of Energy.

selfCheck.q: Which has more potential energy: a 1kg ball at 5m height or a 1kg ball at 10m height?
What happens to the kinetic energy of a car if its speed increases?
At what point in a falling object's path is its kinetic energy at its maximum?
selfCheck.a: Just before it hits the ground (at its highest speed).
